chunks: "The three rules for an ideal op-amp are these. One, the inputs have infinite impedance, so no current flows into either the inverting or non-inverting terminal.
Two, the output has zero impedance, so it acts like an ideal voltage source and can supply whatever current the load wants without the voltage sagging.
Three, the open-loop gain is infinite. The third one is what gives you the famous virtual short.

With negative feedback, the output will do whatever it takes to make the difference between the inputs go to zero, because if there were any difference at all, infinite gain would produce infinite output.
So you can treat the two inputs as being at the same voltage, even though they aren't connected. To use it, say I want an inverting amplifier.
The plus input is grounded, so the minus input is also at zero volts, a virtual ground. The current into the input resistor is V in over R in .
No current goes into the op-amp, so all of it goes through the feedback resistor, and the output is -I R f , so the gain is -R f over R in .
Of course real parts only approximate these: the gain is more like a hundred thousand, bias currents are not zero, and the output impedance is a few tens of ohms open loop."
